body: I think the above issue is a good example of a wider problem with task batching in that executors are implicitly responsible for keeping thread context clean between each task execution in a batch but there is currently no single thing that enforces that. From what I can tell, this is the responsibility of each executor implementation to handle correctly, but it would be great if there were a way to guarantee this invariant in one place, perhaps within the TaskBatcher itself. I looked through a couple instances of batch executors and their structures look largely the similar: `for each task context, possibly modify cluster state, end, return cluster state`. Perhaps a refactoring can remove some boilerplate across the implementations and isolate each task execution with a fresh/restored ThreadContext.

issue.body:
It's possible for a cluster state update task to emit deprecation
warnings, but if the task is executed in a batch then these warnings
will be exposed to the listener for every item in the batch. With this
commit we introduce a mechanism for tasks to capture just the warnings
relevant to them, along with assertions that warnings are not
inadvertently leaked back to the master service.

Closes #85506

body:
The trouble with a general solution is that there is no general pattern for how these executors run. The pattern you mention is actually something of an antipattern (vs updating lower-level things) because of the expense of repeatedly constructing a whole cluster state on each iteration:

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/13bee123ff65419de2e805726ad8d23dfb8d4769/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/cluster/ClusterStateTaskExecutor.java#L28-L31

Executors like `ShardStartedClusterStateTaskExecutor`, `ShardFailedClusterStateTaskExecutor` and `SnapshotsService#SHARD_STATE_EXECUTOR` don't really fit this pattern. But then these executors are unlikely to want to emit any deprecation warnings either.

We can at least detect this kind of leak and give the executor better tools to deal with it, see https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/85525.

Turns out this is trickier than it first appeared. For instance `AllocationService#reroute()` may emit deprecation warnings but we only typically call this once per batch. Which listeners should get those warning headers? Similarly, when opening indices we deduplicate the list of indices first, then iterate over the deduplicated list, so each iteration may correspond with many different task contexts.

issue.body:
Closes #84885

So the test failure from https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/84885 is really interesting. What happens is that one test randomly fails due to the stacktrace below (which IIUC is an issue that @jbaiera is looking into in the general case), but then that kicks off a comedy of errors where everything fails:

```
org.elasticsearch.xpack.enrich.EnrichSecurityIT > testBasicFlowDate FAILED
    org.elasticsearch.client.WarningFailureException: method [PUT], host [http://127.0.0.1:34431/], URI [/my-index/_doc/1?pipeline=my_pipeline], status line [HTTP/1.1 201 Created]
    Warnings: [index name [.monitoring-es-7-2022.03.10] starts with a dot '.', in the next major version, index names starting with a dot are reserved for hidden indices and system indices]
    {"_index":"my-index","_id":"1","_version":1,"result":"created","_shards":{"total":2,"successful":1,"failed":0},"_seq_no":0,"_primary_term":1}
        at app//org.elasticsearch.client.RestClient.convertResponse(RestClient.java:342)
        at app//org.elasticsearch.client.RestClient.performRequest(RestClient.java:312)
        at app//org.elasticsearch.client.RestClient.performRequest(RestClient.java:287)
```

See, since that warning is attached to our request, that results in an exception being thrown, so the pipeline that that test just created is never deleted. Which means that the policy referencing that pipeline cannot be deleted and then subsequent tests can't put a new policy because there's already a non-deleted policy with the same name in place.

That is, once any test in this class fails (and so fails to clean up after itself) then all tests in that class from there on out will fail.

This PR fixes that.

caused by a warning being emitted during auto creation of 'my-index' index.

a warning and that leaks to the index response in this test, which causes
test failures.
